extracted.intended_audience: authors, journal editors, and researchers submitting to or managing medical/biomedical journals
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and guidance for who qualifies as an author or contributor on medical/biomedical journal manuscripts, responsibilities of authors (including corresponding and group authors), handling of acknowledgments, and requirements around use of AI-assisted technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why authorship matters / fairness and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorship confers credit and has important academic, social, and financial implications. Authorship also implies responsibility and accountability for published work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should be aware of the practice of excluding local researchers from low-income and middle-income countries (LMICs) when data are from LMICs; inclusion of local authors adds to fairness, context, and implications of the research and lack of inclusion should prompt questioning and may lead to rejection. Authorship implies taking responsibility and being accountable for what is published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals should implement and publish contributorship policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Because authorship does not communicate what contributions qualified an individual to be an author, some journals now request and publish information about the contributions of each person named as having participated in a submitted study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors are strongly encouraged to develop and implement a contributorship policy. Such policies remove ambiguity about contributions, though they do not resolve the question of quantity/quality of contributions that qualify for authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: ICMJE authorship criteria (the four criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ICMJE recommends that authorship be based on the following 4 criteria: (1) Substantial contributions to the conception or design of the work; or the acquisition, analysis, or interpretation of data for the work; AND (2) Drafting the work or reviewing it critically for important intellectual content; AND (3) Final approval of the version to be published; AND (4) Agreement to be accountable for all aspects of the work in ensuring that questions related to the accuracy or integrity of any part of the work are appropriately investigated and resolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All those designated as authors should meet all four criteria, and all who meet the four criteria should be identified as authors. These criteria reserve authorship status for those who deserve credit and can take responsibility for the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity to meet authorship criteria and limits on misuse
rubrics_metrics.description: The criteria are not intended for use as a means to disqualify colleagues from authorship by denying them the opportunity to meet criterion #s 2 or 3. Therefore, all individuals who meet the first criterion should have the opportunity to participate in the review, drafting, and final approval of the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The individuals who conduct the work are responsible for identifying who meets these criteria and ideally should do so when planning the work, modifying as appropriate as the work progresses. It is the collective responsibility of the authors, not the journal, to determine that all people named as authors meet all four criteria; journal editors should not arbitrate authorship conflicts. If agreement cannot be reached, the institution(s) where the work was performed should be asked to investigate. The criteria used to determine author order may vary and are to be decided collectively by the author group, not by editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors' accountability and knowledge of contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to being accountable for the parts of the work done, an author should be able to identify which co-authors are responsible for specific other parts of the work. In addition, authors should have confidence in the integrity of the contributions of their co-authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must be able to take public responsibility for the work; they will also be expected as individuals to complete disclosure forms. This supports transparency and enables investigation of accuracy or integrity questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corresponding author responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The corresponding author is the one individual who takes primary responsibility for communication with the journal during the manuscript submission, peer-review, and publication process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The corresponding author typically ensures that the journal’s administrative requirements (details of authorship, ethics committee approval, clinical trial registration documentation, disclosures of relationships and activities) are properly completed and reported, although these duties may be delegated. The corresponding author should be available throughout submission and peer-review to respond to editorial queries in a timely way, and after publication to respond to critiques and cooperate with requests for data or additional information. Although the corresponding author has primary responsibility for correspondence, the ICMJE recommends editors send copies of all correspondence to all listed authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large multi-author group authorship rules
rubrics_metrics.description: When a large multi-author group has conducted the work, the group ideally should decide who will be an author before the work is started and confirm who is an author before submitting the manuscript for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All members named as authors should meet all four criteria and be able to take public responsibility for the work. Some large groups designate authorship by a group name, with or without individual names. When submitting a manuscript authored by a group, the corresponding author should specify the group name and clearly identify the group members who can take credit and responsibility for the work as authors. MEDLINE lists as authors whichever names appear on the byline; if the byline includes a group name, MEDLINE will list individual group members as authors or collaborators only if a note associated with the byline clearly states where individual names appear and whether those names are authors or collaborators. Group members will be expected to complete disclosure forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-author contributors and acknowledgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributors who meet fewer than all 4 of the above criteria for authorship should not be listed as authors, but they should be acknowledged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of activities that alone do NOT qualify for authorship: acquisition of funding; general supervision of a research group or general administrative support; writing assistance, technical editing, language editing, and proofreading. Those whose contributions do not justify authorship may be acknowledged individually or together under a heading (e.g., 'Clinical Investigators' or 'Participating Investigators'); their contributions should be specified (e.g., 'served as scientific advisors,' 'collected data,' 'provided and cared for study patients'). Because acknowledgment may imply endorsement, editors are advised to require that the corresponding author obtain written permission from all acknowledged individuals. Use of AI for writing assistance should be reported in the acknowledgment section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of AI-assisted technology use and related rules
rubrics_metrics.description: At submission, the journal should require authors to disclose whether they used artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted technologies (such as LLMs, chatbots, or image creators) in the production of submitted work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors who use AI should describe in the cover letter and the submitted work how they used it: writing assistance should be described in the acknowledgment section; AI used for data collection, analysis, or figure generation should be described in the methods. Chatbots (e.g., ChatGPT) should not be listed as authors because they cannot be responsible for accuracy, integrity, and originality. Humans are responsible for any material that included AI-assisted technologies and should carefully review and edit AI output because it can be incorrect, incomplete, or biased. Authors should not cite AI as an author, must be able to assert there is no plagiarism (including in AI-produced text and images), and must ensure appropriate attribution of quoted material including full citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes to authorship after submission or publication
rubrics_metrics.description: If authors request removal or addition of an author after manuscript submission or publication, journal editors should seek an explanation and signed statement of agreement for the requested change from all listed authors and from the author to be removed or added.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should document and require signed agreement from all parties involved to approve post-submission or post-publication authorship changes, ensuring transparency and preventing inappropriate changes.
